newsitem.title: UK: Pension fund overseas assets face new law threat.
newsitem.headline: Pension fund overseas assets face new law threat.

text.p: A newly enacted law to safeguard pensions may cause British pension fund managers to cut their overseas investments, experts say.
They said the Minimum Funding Requirement (MFR), in force since April, puts British pension funds with overseas holdings at risk of being judged underfunded.
"There is quite a high likelihood that pension fund managers will switch out of foreign securities," said Ken Ayers of consultants Frank Russell.

MFR values pension funds based on the average age of members - if the age is high there is a valuation based on a high proportion of UK gilts, if young then a higher proportion of UK equities is used.
If overseas investments underperform UK gilts and equities, a pension fund could find itself breaching the MFR, according to Tony Osborne-Barker of consultants William M. Mercer.
Pension funds with ageing membership and high UK equity holdings could also feel compelled to switch into gilts, he said.

"If pension funds change their asset allocation to minimise the risk of movement in market value relative to MFR...then there will be a significant movement into UK gilts, and out of property and overseas equity and bonds," said Paul Haines, investment director at Sedgwick Noble Lowndes.
But a large fund flow into UK gilts - which historically underperform UK and foreign equities - could prove expensive for pension funds, experts say, and increase their long-term need for funding.
British pension funds have moved strongly in recent years to diversify holdings and have poured billion of dollars into overseas markets.
As of March, British funds had an average of just over 25 percent of holdings in overseas equities and bonds, according to figures produced by WM Company.
To be sure, a wholesale dumping of overseas holdings is not likely, experts say.

"Pension funds have no choice but to take MFR's on board, but trustees are looking for ways that don't impact asset allocations and returns," said Eric Lambert, senior investment consultant at WM Company.
He believes that pension funds recognise the strong returns achieved through overseas.
Many pension funds have MFR surpluses, Lambert says, and will likely feel free to allocate assets for higher returns.
But those with some risk of breaching MFR may decide to turn to defined contribution pension systems, under which companies contribute a fixed amount, Haines said.
